title: THE STRUCTURAL MAPPING
subtitle: Where game theory illuminates nuclear strategy — and where it misleads.
source: Schelling, T. (1960). The Strategy of Conflict; Axelrod, R. (1984). The Evolution of Cooperation.

sourceElements.label: Mutual Defection
sourceElements.description: Both betray → both receive maximum sentence.

sourceElements.label: Cooperation
sourceElements.description: Both stay silent → shared gain, lowest joint cost.

sourceElements.label: Dominant Strategy
sourceElements.description: Defect regardless of what the other player does.

sourceElements.label: One-Shot Game
sourceElements.description: Played once; no shadow of the future.

targetElements.label: Mutual Strike
targetElements.description: Both launch → both destroyed; no winner.

targetElements.label: Détente
targetElements.description: Mutual restraint → shared stability, arms-reduction gains.

targetElements.label: First-Strike Logic
targetElements.description: Strike first before the adversary can retaliate.

targetElements.label: Indefinitely Repeated
targetElements.description: Nations interact across decades; reputation compounds.

breakNote: The analogy breaks at repeated-game dynamics. Nuclear deterrence is indefinitely iterated — reputations compound, reciprocity is possible, and cooperation can emerge from repeated interaction (Axelrod 1984). The classical PD is one-shot: no shadow of the future, no reputation, no Tit-for-Tat equilibrium. Applying PD to deterrence without this correction understates the stability of nuclear peace.
